title: Think in Ufuncs
blurb: One ufunc call replaces a thousand iterations: clip, band, and window whole signals at once.

cells.title: One call, every element
cells.body:
A ufunc ('universal function') applies one operation to an entire array in compiled code: np.maximum(v, 0) clamps every element, v * 2 + 1 is two full-array passes, and np.sqrt(np.abs(v)) chains three. There is no visible loop because the loop is inside numpy, over contiguous memory.

The reasoning shift: stop asking 'how do I iterate?' and start asking 'which whole-array transformation maps my input to my output?'. Most day-one loops — scale, offset, clip, negate, compare — are each a single ufunc expression. This notebook trains the next tier: branching with np.where and windowed reductions with cumulative sums.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

v = np.array([-1.0, 0.5, 2.0, 4.5])
print(np.maximum(v, 0.0))     # elementwise clamp at zero
print(v * 2 + 1)              # two whole-array passes
print(np.sqrt(np.abs(v)))

cells.title: np.where is an array-valued if/else
cells.body:
np.where(cond, x, y) evaluates both branches as arrays and then picks elementwise: cond[i] true yields x[i], else y[i]. Nesting them builds priority ladders: the outermost condition claims its cells first, and whatever it rejects falls through to the inner expression.

Order matters when categories overlap. A banding rule like 'code 3 if v is at least 3.6, else code 2 if v is at least 3.3, else...' must be written consistently from one end of the ladder: each condition must be complete for its band, otherwise cells fall through to the wrong branch. Getting the boundary comparisons right (>= vs >) is the classic off-by-one of banding.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

v = np.array([2.9, 3.1, 3.4, 3.9])
code = np.where(v >= 3.6, 3,
       np.where(v >= 3.3, 2,
       np.where(v >= 3.0, 1, 0)))
print(code)
print(np.where(v < 3.2, 'low', 'high'))   # branches can be strings

cells.title: np.diff turns a signal into its change points
cells.body:
np.diff(x) is the array of consecutive differences: element i is x[i+1] - x[i], and the result is one shorter than the input. That single definition converts 'when did something change?' into 'where is the difference array nonzero?' — the same move as calculus, where questions about levels become questions about slopes.

Combine it with a threshold comparison and you can count crossings: cast a boolean above/below array to int, and an upward crossing is exactly a +1 step in that indicator — a one-liner that replaces scanning the signal with a loop. The same skeleton counts downcrossings, toggles, or 'any switch'.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([0, 0, 5, 5, 0, 5, 5])
over = (x >= 5).astype(int)
print(np.diff(over))                    # +1 marks an upcrossing
print(np.count_nonzero(np.diff(over) == 1))

exercise.title: Saturating ADC
exercise.statement:
An analog-to-digital converter is only trustworthy inside its rails: readings below lo or above hi have already clipped (saturated) at the rail value, and the downstream filter expects exactly that.

Implement clamp(x, lo, hi): given a 1-D int64 array x and plain ints lo <= hi, return a 1-D int64 array of the same length where every value below lo is replaced by lo and every value above hi by hi — one vectorized call, no loops.
constraints: x is 1-D int64 with at least 1 element; lo <= hi are plain ints
the result is 1-D int64 with the same length; every value lies in [lo, hi]

examples.why: -3 clips up to 0 and 12 clips down to 10; the middle readings pass through
values already inside the rails are untouched

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def clamp(x, lo, hi):
    """Saturate x into [lo, hi], elementwise.

    x is 1-D int64; lo and hi are plain ints with lo <= hi.
    """
    pass
hints: You could write a loop with an if/elif/else per element — but there is a single numpy call whose entire job is 'push every value into an interval'. What is it called?
np.clip(x, lo, hi) applies the clamp elementwise in compiled code; plain Python ints for lo and hi broadcast against the int64 array without changing its dtype.
return np.clip(x, lo, hi). That is the whole function: length, dtype and values are preserved by the ufunc.
exercise.reasoning: Clipping is the canonical job where the loop version and the ufunc version differ enormously in speed and readability. np.clip composes minimum and maximum — clamp above, then below — and preserves dtype and shape, which is why the int64 contract holds without any casting in your code. The transferable habit: before writing an elementwise if ladder, scan the ufunc list (clip, maximum, abs, sign, around). A surprising share of 'per element' logic is already a named function — and when it is, the named version is both faster and self-documenting.

exercise.title: Voltage Bands
exercise.statement:
A battery stack reports cell voltages. Operations classifies each cell into one of four bands, with exact boundary semantics:

  • band 0: v < 3.0 — critical
  • band 1: 3.0 <= v < 3.3 — low
  • band 2: 3.3 <= v < 3.6 — nominal
  • band 3: v >= 3.6 — full

Implement voltage_zone(v): return the per-cell band codes as a 1-D int64 array of the same length, built with nested np.where (or np.select). No loops. Every interval is half-open on the right, and band 0 catches everything below 3.0 — including negative readings.
constraints: v is 1-D float64 with at least 1 element; values may be negative
the result is 1-D int64, same length
boundaries are exact: 3.0 is band 1, 3.3 is band 2, 3.6 is band 3

examples.why: one cell in each band, no cell on a boundary
the three boundary values land in the band above them: 1, 2, 3

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def voltage_zone(v):
    """Map each voltage to its band code 0..3.

    Bands: 0 v<3.0; 1 3.0<=v<3.3; 2 3.3<=v<3.6; 3 v>=3.6.
    Returns int64 codes, same length as v.
    """
    pass
hints: Four bands but only three decisions: if you check thresholds from the top down, what does the innermost else branch have to catch?
Nest np.where outside-in on the upper edges: np.where(v >= 3.6, 3, np.where(v >= 3.3, 2, np.where(v >= 3.0, 1, 0))). Each true test claims its cell; the final else is band 0.
Finish with .astype(np.int64) so the code dtype is a contract, not an accident of int promotion: code = nested wheres; return code.astype(np.int64).
exercise.reasoning: A band ladder is a sequence of half-open intervals, and nested np.where encodes it as priority from the outside in: the outermost test (v ≥ 3.6) claims its cells first; whatever it rejects falls to the next test, so each inner condition only needs to separate its band from the ones below it. That is why three thresholds define four bands — the last branch is the remainder, and it automatically catches negatives and anything below 3.0. The boundary semantics (3.0 → band 1, not band 0) come from using >= at each edge; this is the classic off-by-one of banding, and the boundary-visible test pins it. The trailing .astype(np.int64) makes the output dtype a contract rather than an implementation detail.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def voltage_zone(v):
    """Map each voltage to its band code 0..3."""
    v = np.asarray(v)
    code = np.where(v >= 3.6, 3,
           np.where(v >= 3.3, 2,
           np.where(v >= 3.0, 1, 0)))
    return code.astype(np.int64)

exercise.title: Count the Upcrossings
exercise.statement:
A relay triggers when a monitored signal rises onto or above a trip level. An upward crossing at position i means: x[i] < level and x[i+1] >= level. Touching the level from below counts; sliding along above it does not.

Implement count_upcrossings(x, level): return the number of upward crossings as a plain integer, computed from np.diff of a 0/1 indicator — no loops, no sign scans.
constraints: x is 1-D numeric (int64 or float64) with at least 1 element; level is a plain number
upcrossing at i means x[i] < level and x[i+1] >= level
a signal of length 1 has 0 crossings (no adjacent pair exists)

examples.why: the signal rises onto the level at positions 0 and 2
the signal never reaches the level, so nothing crosses

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def count_upcrossings(x, level):
    """Count positions i with x[i] < level and x[i+1] >= level.

    Returns a plain integer; x may be int64 or float64.
    """
    pass
hints: Convert the level question into a 0/1 question first: over = (x >= level). What does np.diff(over.astype(int)) look like at a crossing, and what values does it take elsewhere?
over is 1 at-or-above the level and 0 below; np.diff of that int indicator is +1 exactly at an upcrossing (0 to 1), -1 at a downcrossing, and 0 while the signal stays on one side.
over = (np.asarray(x) >= level).astype(np.int64); return int(np.count_nonzero(np.diff(over) == 1)). The == 1 keeps only upward transitions.
exercise.reasoning: Level questions become edge questions once you replace the signal by a 0/1 indicator: over[i] answers 'is sample i at or above the level?'. np.diff of that indicator is +1 precisely where the indicator steps 0→1 — which is the definition of an upcrossing, including the 'touching counts' rule, because the indicator uses >=. This is the discrete-derivative view: a threshold event is a property of the change array, not of the level array, and counting events becomes counting pattern matches. The same skeleton counts downcrossings (== -1), toggles, or 'any switch' (!= 0) — one idiom for every 'how many times did it flip?' question in sensor and event data.

exercise.title: Moving Average by Cumulative Sum
exercise.statement:
A smoothing pass replaces each full window of w consecutive samples by its mean — a valid moving average: the output has len(x) - w + 1 entries, with no partial windows at the edges.

Implement moving_average(x, w): return a 1-D float64 array of length n - w + 1 where entry i is mean(x[i:i+w]), each value rounded to 4 decimal places. Compute every window sum from a single cumulative sum — np.cumsum plus one subtraction of two shifted views. No loops, no np.convolve, no per-window .mean() calls.
constraints: the output length is exactly len(x) - w + 1 (valid windows only)
entry i is the mean of x[i:i+w], as float64 rounded to 4 decimal places

examples.why: four valid windows of width 2: means 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5
the widest legal window covers everything: a single mean, output length 1

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def moving_average(x, w):
    """Valid-window moving average via one cumulative sum.

    x is 1-D int64, 1 <= w <= len(x); the result has length
    len(x) - w + 1 and is rounded to 4 decimal places.
    """
    pass
hints: Window i's sum is c[i+w] - c[i] if c is the cumulative sum with a 0 prepended. Why must the 0 be prepended, and how long is c?
c = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(x))) has length n+1; then (c[w:] - c[:-w]) is the vector of all window sums at once — for w=1 it degenerates to c[1:] - c[:-1], which is x itself.
x = np.asarray(x, dtype=np.float64); c = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(x))); return np.round((c[w:] - c[:-w]) / w, 4).
exercise.reasoning: The cumulative sum turns range sums into two array reads: with a 0 prepended, c[k] is the total of the first k samples, so the sum of window i is c[i+w] - c[i] — and slicing c[w:] against c[:-w] produces all n-w+1 window sums in one subtraction. Total cost: one cumsum pass plus one vectorized subtract-divide, instead of touching every window separately (w times more work) or looping in Python. The prepended 0 is what makes the first window work with no special case: window 0 needs 'the sum of nothing before the array began'. This prefix-sum trick underlies running totals, range queries, box filters and integral images — anywhere 'sum of a slice' gets asked more than once.
